#Q1 hypothesis: The yield of cereals is affected by six variables: 1) mean number of overwintering plants, 2) mean number of ears, 3) pH of the soil, 4) content of phosphorus, 5) content of potassium, and 6) content of magnesium.

#Q2 variables: There are seven variables: yield, winter, ears, pH, P, K, and Mg. All seven variables are numerical and composed of continuous data. 

#Q3 types of variables: The response variable (dependent variable) is the yield. The focal predictors (independent variables) are the other six variables -- winter, ears, pH, P, K, and Mg -- depending on which is being plotted for a given graph. The covariates are winter, ears, pH, P, K, and Mg, but dependent on which variable is being plotted as the independent.

#The below dot charts, boxplots, and histograms are mainly for my own practice.

#Feel free to skim through to the scatterplots.

#Dot Charts:
> dotchart(wheat$yield, xlab = 'Yield')
> dotchart(wheat$winter, xlab = 'Overwinter')
> dotchart(wheat$ears, xlab = 'Ears of Wheat')

> plot(wheat[,c(1,7)], xlab = 'Yield', ylab = 'Magnesium (Mg)', main = 'Yield vs. Magnesium (Mg)')

#Comments on Observed Patterns:
#Generally, when each of the six covariates -- winter, ears, pH, P, K, and Mg -- are analyzed as the focal predictor to the response variable -- yield -- the greater the value of the focal predictor, the greater the yield of wheat. However, there are some exceptions. 

#Yield vs. pH has an inverse relationship where, when the pH fell, the yield of wheat generally increased. Yield vs. Phosphorus (P) indicates that the greatest yield of wheat occurred when phosphorus was between 70-90 mg/kg. For Yield vs. Potassium (K), the greatest yield of wheat occurred when potassium was about 100 mg/kg, though there are a couple of outliers near, and greater than, 300 mg/kg potassium. With Yield vs. Magnesium (Mg), the data is far more widespread, where values of 45 up to ~80 mg/kg of magnesium can all produce high yields of wheat. 

#Overall, these data indicate that the greater the overwinter and ears of wheat survival rates, the greater the yield of wheat. Additionally, optimal mg/kg of the elements phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium in the soil, can also increase the yield of wheat. The pH of the soil is the one variable that, when at lower values, results in a greater yield of wheat.
